 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT The Road to ‘Rocky’: Making the Underdog Biopic Had Its Struggles, Too
 “I Play Rocky,” which revisits Sylvester Stallone’s breakout role, became a surprise festival hit this year. But getting it made was a long-shot undertaking.
 Listen · 7:52 min Share full article 
 19 
 The actor Anthony Ippolito, playing a young Sylvester Stallone, bonds with his canine co-star in the movie “I Play Rocky.” Credit... Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios By Clarissa Cruz 
 Nov. 12, 2026 Updated 1:47 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda. Add The New York Times as a preferred source on Google Agrega The New York Times como fuente preferida en Google › 
 “I Play Rocky” is all kinds of meta. In the new movie about the making of the beloved 1976 sports drama “Rocky,” art imitates life on as many levels as the Philadelphia Museum of Art has steps. Sure, it’s the story of how the then-struggling actor Sylvester Stallone wrote a script about a struggling boxer named Rocky Balboa — and insisted on starring in the film, despite his sparse credentials and the fact that producers were throwing increasing amounts of money at him to walk away.
 But it could also be about Peter Gamble, the longtime ghostwriter who penned the screenplay for “I Play Rocky” eight years ago, yearning to get a script with his name actually on it made into a movie. Then there’s Anthony Ippolito, an actor so determined to play the young Stallone that he sent a self-taped audition to filmmakers before he even saw a script. And finally, there’s the director Peter Farrelly, no stranger to success after his 2019 best picture winner, “Green Book,” but still feeling the sting after his Academy win became tinged with controversy . Each, in some way or another, are like Rocky: underdogs fighting for a chance to be seen.
 Well, we know how that first part turned out. “Rocky” was a commercial and critical knockout, grossing $225 million worldwide ($1.33 billion in today’s money), nabbing 10 Oscar nominations and winning three including best picture, and bringing instant fame for its star, a then-30-year-old Stallone.
 The outlook for the movie-about-the-movie looks pretty rosy, too. “I Play Rocky” got an enthusiastic reception when it debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival in September, and reviews have been mostly positive since, singling out both Ippolito’s transformative performance and the movie’s triumphant, crowd-pleasing tone.
 Image The “I Play Rocky” director Peter Farrelly recreated many scenes from “Rocky,” including the climactic boxing match between Rocky and Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers, who is here played by Stephan James). Credit... Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios Speaking two weeks before the Nov. 20 nationwide release of “I Play Rocky” and a few days after the midterm elections, Farrelly, 69, was giddy. “I don’t want to get into politics, but the last three days have been some of the happiest days of my life,” he said on a Zoom call from New York. “It gave me and a lot of people hope again. And this is a movie that gives you hope and inspires you.”
